---
title: "Request file"
---

The request file, `request.yaml`, contains the instructions for requesting a
subset of data from a data package. The file is created by a Requester through
the web application, terminal interface, or even manually (though not
recommended). The file is used by an Owner to check and generate the requested
data subset. You can
[read more about the Requester and Owner user types in the Design overview page](/docs/design/interface/inputs.qmd)

The request file is intended to be both human-readable and machine-readable. It
should be simple enough for a Requester to understand and, when needed, edit
manually. At the same time, it should be structured enough that Propagate can
check it against the data package metadata and convert it into an SQL query for
generating the requested data subset.

## Format

The request file uses YAML. YAML was chosen because it is more readable for
manual editing than JSON and less verbose than TOML for lists of columns and row
conditions.

## Structure

The request file contains the following top-level sections:

- The top level contains information about this specific request.
- `requester`: Information about the person requesting the data.
- `project`: Information about the research project that requires the data.
- `data-package`: Information about the data package the request applies to.
- `subsets`: The requested data subsets, with one item per resource.

Each of these is elaborated on below:

### Top level

The top level includes information about the request itself, such as when and
why it was created. This helps an Owner organize and track requests, which is
especially beneficial for data packages that receive large volumes of requests.

```{.yaml}
datetime-modified: "DATETIME"
datetime-created: "DATETIME"
datetime-modified: "DATETIME"
motivation: "TEXT"
```

- `datetime-created`: When the first iteration of the request was created.
  - The format should be ISO 8601, e.g. `2026-07-06T01:45:34Z` of the current
    time without time zone information. Propagate assumes that it is very rare
    that Requesters are outside of the Owner's timezone and that it is mostly
    used by people within the same group or institution that are assumed to be
    using Propagate together.
- `datetime-modified`: When the request was last modified. This can act as an ID
  which facilitates referring to a specific iteration of a request, e.g. in
  dialog between the Owner and Requester. Precision to the second should be
  sufficient. The value is recorded in UTC using the same ISO 8601 format as
  `datetime-created`.
  - This field is automatically populated when the request is saved via a user
    interface (be it the web app or the TUI). If the request is edited manually,
    it must be updated manually.
- `motivation`: Explanation for why the requester's project needs access to this
  data subset. This is used by the Owner to check whether the requested data is
  relevant to the project. The motivation is particularly needed for human
  health data since there are legal requirements (e.g. GDPR) to declare for what
  purposes the data is used.

### Requester

The `requester` section describes who is requesting the data. This person
doesn't strictly have to be the one working with the data, but they should serve
as the main point of contact for the Owner.

```{.yaml}
requester:
  name: "TEXT"
  email: "TEXT"
```

- `name`: The name of the requester.
- `email`: The email of the requester.

### Project

The `project` section contains information about the research project that
requires the data. A project is defined as a body of work that results in a
research output, e.g. a paper, report, website, dashboard, or analysis. This
could be a part of a PhD student's thesis or a collaboration research project
for a group of researchers. This field is necessary to ensure that the data
requested is aligned with what it is intended to be used for, which can be a
legal requirement (e.g. in GDPR).

```{.yaml}
project:
  name: "TEXT"
  title: "TEXT"
  description: "TEXT"
```

- `name`: Think of name as a GitHub repository name, which is meant for
  consumption by both humans and machines. Use lowercase letters and hyphens
  where possible, e.g. `my-research-project`. `name` is meant to be an indirect
  identifier which needs to be combined with other information such as data
  package, requester, and project name to uniquely identify a request. It is
  also meant to be legible enough to display in different areas/different ways.
- `title`: A longer human-readable project title, e.g. `My research project`.
  This could be used by the Owner to publicly display the data package requests.
- `description`: A summary of the project, including details like background,
  rationale, basic methods, and potential research questions. This information,
  combined with the `motivation`, is mainly to help the Owner ensure that the
  data requested matches what it will be used for.

### Data package

The `data-package` section identifies the data package the request applies to.
This information will be automatically populated from the data package metadata
when creating a request via the web application or the TUI.

```{.yaml}
data-package:
  name: "TEXT"
  version: "X.Y.Z"
```

- `name`: A human readable name to refer to. It is lowercased and doesn't
  include any spaces. E.g., `my-data-package`.
- `version`: Helps the Owner detect which version of the data package the
  request is for.

### Subsets

The `subsets` section describes the data the Requester would like to obtain. It
is a sequence with one item for each requested resource. Note that the subset
section is not intended to allow for a general-purpose query syntax, e.g. the
request format should not support joins, grouping, arbitrary functions, random
sampling, or row selection by position.

```{.yaml}
subsets:
  - resource: "RESOURCE-NAME-1"
    columns:
      - "COLUMN-NAME-1"
      - "COLUMN-NAME-2"
    rows:
      - column: "COLUMN-NAME-1"
        operator: "OPERATOR"
        value: "VALUE-TO-COMPARE-AGAINST"
        not: "BOOLEAN"
  - resource: "RESOURCE-NAME-2"
    columns:
      - "COLUMN-NAME"
    rows:
      - column: "COLUMN-NAME"
        operator: "OPERATOR"
        value: "VALUE-TO-COMPARE-AGAINST"
        not: "BOOLEAN"
```

Each subset contains:

- `resource`: The name of the data resource to subset. A resource can only be
  included once in a request and for each resource specified, a separate data
  table will be outputted.
- `columns`: The columns to include from the resource. Each list item must be
  exactly one column name. Regex and SQL-like shorthands are not supported,
  which keeps the request simple and avoids parsing unsafe queries.
  - If `columns` is empty or not included, all columns from the resource are
    included.
  - As expected from the YAML structure, the specified columns are just applied
    to the resource they are listed under; columns with the same name in other
    resource will not be included unless they are explicitly listed under each
    resource.
- `rows`: The conditions used to select rows from the resource. All listed
  conditions must be met for a row to be included.
  - If `rows` is empty or not included, all rows from the resource are included.
  - Contrary to how `columns` work, the row conditions are combined **across**
    resources rather than only applied to the resource they are listed under. In
    other words, the rows that are kept represent the statistical units that
    meet all the row condition listed under all the resources. This is
    elaborated on with an example at the end of the next section.

#### Row conditions

Row conditions use a structured key-value mapping instead of free-form SQL. This
maps closely to controls in the web application and TUI and makes it easier to
check manually edited files for unsupported operators.


Each row condition contains:

- `column`: The name of the column to use for the comparison.
- `operator`: How to compare the column against the reference value. The
  initially supported operators are:
  - Equality: `=`
  - Comparisons: `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`
  - Membership: `IN`
  - Missing values: `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`
- `value`: The reference value to compare against. This is not needed for
  operators that check for missing values. For the `IN` operator it needs to be
  a list of values.
- `not`: Invert the condition.
  - E.g. if using `=` and setting `not: true` then all rows NOT matching the
    reference value will be returned.
  - Note that one slightly inconsistent aspect in SQL is that `NOT` is a prefix
    to negating all operators except `IS NULL` where it is advised to use the
    special operator `IS NOT NULL` rather than `NOT` + `IS NULL` because of how
    null comparisons work in SQL. The most consistent user experience would be
    to still use `not: true` and that we take care of converting that to the
    operator `IS NOT NULL` behind the scenes, but if that seems complicated we
    can also introduce this special operator to the user.

As mentioned above, all the row conditions used to select a subset of
statistical/observational units (e.g. individuals) will be applied to all the
resources together rather than individually to each reasource. This is for GDPR
purposes (and other legal/privacy regulations) and for statistical reasons.

For example, if in a survey a condition is `Gender == "Man"`, and in another
resource biometrics that doesn't have a condition, the subsetted participant IDs
from the survey will be applied to the biometrics, so that all resources contain
the same set of participants. This is a legal thing, as much as a statistical
thing since nearly all statistical methods require the same observational units
within the data (e.g. minimal missingness). It's to ensure that the researcher
is only given the data that they need for the analysis, as described in the
motivation. Like the principle of "least permissions" but in a data context.

### A complete example

A complete request file might look like this.

```{.yaml}
datetime-created: "2026-07-04T01:44:34Z"
datetime-modified: "2026-07-06T01:45:34Z"
motivation: |
  Explanation of why the data is needed.

requester:
  name: "First Last"
  email: "firstlast@example.org"
  motivation: |
    We would like access to metabolic and block variables to evaluate
    our hypothesis regarding ...

project:
  name: "metabolic-cost"
  title: "Metabolic cost estimation"
  description: |
    Our project investigates the gas exchange during metabolism
    with the aim to determine ...

data-package:
  name: "example-seed-beetle"
  version: "0.5.1"

subsets:
  - resource: "metabolism"
    columns:
      - "strain"
      - "activity"
    rows:
      - column: "age"
        operator: ">="
        value: "20"
      - column: "age"
        operator: "<="
        value: "40"
  - resource: "something-else"
    columns:
      - "col2"
    rows:
      - column: "col2"
        operator: "is null"
        not: "true"
      - column: "color"
        operator: "IN"
        value: ["A", "B", "C"]
```
